rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Per-exercise leap test — 3 observable Monday outcomes.
rules_evaluated.evidence: L118-121: three falsifiable outcomes named ('Writes a failing test that proves the bug exists', 'Pushes back on at least one line in a diff', 'Runs root-cause interrogation before accepting Claude's first fix'), each paired with a concrete falsifiability test (commit history showing a test commit before/with the fix; scrollback or commit body showing a line-level objection; scrollback showing a root-cause turn before any commit). Named verbs, not abstract competencies — a working engineer can self-check each on their own codebase.

Maintainer 'Watch-fors' (L102-104) names two dominant failure modes with escape hatches: 'Tests-skipped' (student jumps straight to a fix) → trainer push 'back up — what's the failing test that would prove this bug exists?'; 'Diff rubber-stamp' (student says 'looks fine' under 30 seconds) → trainer push 'find me one line you'd have written differently.' Both forcing functions (test-first, push-back) have a named failure mode and a named recovery move.

Trace (regenerated 2026-08-26 against current body_sha) scores mood_score 8/8 for the single phase and 8/8 at close, any_below_8: false. Emotional state: joyful creation ('it works, on my repo') carried through test-write, push-back, interrogation, and ship — sets up close-the-ticket per trace close.mood_note.

No shame-framing anywhere in body — 'push back' (L26), 'interrogate' (L29,33), 'digging' (L45) are all framed as the student's own curiosity/judgment, never as correcting a mistake the student made. M1's mood is joy, not unease, so the unease-specific epistemic/punitive distinction this rule targets doesn't have a live case here, but the general no-shame check passes on a close read.
